lines.text: Every electric car battery needs lithium.
And California believes it's sitting on a huge supply, under a desert lake called the Salton Sea.
The question is whether we can get it out without making the air worse for the people who live there.
The Salton Sea is California's largest lake, in the southern desert.
The lithium here isn't dug out of rock. It's dissolved in hot, salty brine, deep underground.
Geothermal plants already pump that brine up to make electricity. A new step would pull the lithium out, then send the brine back down.
But there's a catch. The Salton Sea is shrinking.
As the water pulls back, it leaves dry lakebed behind. And on windy days, that lakebed turns to dust.
Lithium plants need water too. In August 2026, a court ruled the biggest project's review hadn't shown how its water use could affect the air.
So who breathes that air? Let's map it.
California scores every census tract for health and pollution burden. Around the sea, that's seventy-nine tracts.
Twenty of them rank in the state's worst fifteen percent for asthma emergency visits. All twenty are in Imperial County.
Next, the dust itself. Eight EPA monitors around the sea measure coarse dust, called P M ten.
From 2023 through 2025, at least one of them went over the federal health limit on seventy-one different days.
Bad days peak in spring and early fall. But a monitor can't tell if the dust came from the lakebed, the desert, or a farm field.
This is where GeoAI comes in: artificial intelligence that learns from maps and images.
Drones can't extract lithium, but they can watch the ground, flying low to label which lakebed is crusted, and which is loose.
A model learns from those labels, then applies them to satellite images of the entire shoreline.
The goal: add wind data, and forecast bad dust days one to three days ahead, so schools and clinics can prepare.
But a model is only useful if it works in places it hasn't seen.
So instead of testing on random points, we hold out whole stretches of shoreline. If it fails there, it isn't ready.
Then we compare solutions, downsides included.
At Owens Lake, flooding the dry lakebed cut dust by more than ninety-nine percent. But it cost over two and a half billion dollars, and about sixty thousand acre-feet of water a year.
Gravel needs no water, but tons of rock. Habitat ponds help birds, but the state has finished only about a sixth of its 2028 goal.
No single fix wins. The models help decide which patch of lakebed gets which fix.
Finally, the models run scenarios: no new lithium, one big project, or full build-out, with and without dust control.
That way, we can compare futures before anything is built.
Lithium and clean air don't have to be a trade-off. But only if we measure.
The full plan, the interactive maps, and all the code are free to explore. Links are in the description.
